work.title: Canones (In Pauli Apostoli Epistula Canones A Peregrino Episcopo)

paragraphs.text: Taken up with many pressing needs, I have been slow to answer your letter, dearest friend. You had asked me to search the divine scriptures carefully and find some very strong bulwark against the cunning deceit of the heretics. You wanted it to be neat and elegant rather than long or tedious, so that it might more quickly overthrow the impudence of those who, when the truest testimonies are put before them, strive to twist them into their own most perverse sense, or else deny that they are written at all. So you say that something must be devised against them that does not swell with an orator's crafty eloquence or get tangled in the slippery syllogisms of dialectic, for these are often the chief refuges of certain people. Instead you want something that shines with pure truth and rests on the wonderful authority of the scriptures. You also say that whatever is contrary and hostile to the spiritual and innocent Christian faith must be avoided, since it is the wisdom of the world and the apostle called it foolishness. I heard this from you very often, and you wrote to me other things like it, so it seemed fitting to me to set the scriptures themselves in plain view, that is, the fourteen epistles of the most blessed apostle Paul. In their text I have marked off the sense of each testimony and numbered the testimonies, writing these numbers above them in ink for each epistle in order, beginning from one and running to the end of its length. Then, picking out certain words from the testimonies themselves, I composed canons that keep the same savour as those testimonies. Beneath these canons I have noted the titles of the epistles and the numbers of the testimonies, so that wherever, or whichever, testimony you are looking for, you may find it very easily through the canon under which it is placed. The canons have their own numbers written in red: ninety canons for the fourteen epistles. You will find these numbers written above the matching testimonies throughout the whole text of scripture, namely at the point from which a few words seem necessary for each canon. Note carefully why a canon does not contain the whole testimony: the testimonies consist of many verses, but the canons of a few words, because a few words are always what is brought forward in a reply. So it happens that for some testimonies only the beginning agrees with the canon under which they are placed, for others the middle, for some the end, and very often the whole. For that reason you will find the numbers of two, three or more canons written in red above a single testimony, but, as I have said, at the point from which a few words seem necessary for each. I want you to understand that I have laboured at this in order to set out faithfully the content of the scriptures, as an enemy to no one, and so that, as you asked, the minds of those who err may be corrected more quickly. Farewell in Christ!

That God is true. God is also spirit, and the God of the ages, who possesses immortality and is invisible, dwelling in unapproachable light. He is also king and lord, and Christ is his image and firstborn, in whom there is not found 'yes and no', but only 'yes'.
Which things are discordant and hostile to one another in their motion and their fruits; for there is a crooked generation, and perdition too has its own son.
That there are two kinds of spirits: one of God, the other of the world, leading to error.
That there are two wisdoms: one of God, the other of human beings, or of the flesh.
That many are called gods: for some their belly is their god, and so are the spirits of this air and the powers of darkness, and also the elements of the world.
That sins or demons are called darkness, or works of darkness, by the apostle.
That it belongs to the foolish, the carnal or the doubting to think or feel crudely about the divinity.
That all things are from God and in God, who works all things; that every fatherhood is named from him; and that all things were created through Christ.
That wisdom, grace and blessing are spiritual gifts, and that his invisible attributes are understood and seen through the things that have been made.
That the judgements of God are unsearchable and his ways past finding out; and so too the riches of Christ and his manifold wisdom.
That the things that are seen are temporal, but the things that are not seen are eternal; and that therefore those who hope only in this life are the most pitiable of all people.

That Christ took on the likeness of sinful flesh in his ministry. In him are the treasures of wisdom; he made the two one, and ascending on high he led captivity captive; and the apostle said that he no longer knew him according to the flesh.
That Christ, who died in the flesh for us, is both man and God, the mediator between God and human beings.
That Christ is the foundation of the apostolic faith. He is the cornerstone and our head, from whom the whole body grows, and in whom those who believe the gospel are built up.
That the mystery once hidden from the children of men has now been revealed to the saints through the apostle; and that Christ is called the wisdom which none of the rulers of this world knew.

That Christ the Son of God is the image, the power and the wisdom of the Father; that in him the fullness of the divinity dwells bodily; and that he alone in the flesh knew no sin, while every human being is a liar.
That the man Christ is called God and Lord by the apostle; and that he is said to have been made, not in his divinity, but from the seed of David and from a woman.
That Christ is our peace, and that therefore on his cross he dissolved the enmity and blotted out the bond that stood against us, breaking down the dividing wall.
Canon XIX. That Christ fulfilled the Father's will in his passion not against his will but of his own will, humbling himself even to death.
That the heavenly Jerusalem is free; that we are counted as the offspring according to the promises made to Isaac; and that Christ is the head and fullness of the church.

That the Spirit of God searches all things and knows even the depths of God, which only the spiritual understand and speak of; they judge all things, but they themselves are judged by no one, and they will go out to meet Christ.
That sin brings death and reduces the soul to slavery.
That ignorance is darkness, but knowledge is light in the Lord, and each has its own children.
That before the ages God predestined the wisdom hidden in a mystery for our glory, that is, the glory of those whom he chose before the foundation of the world.

That it is by the grace and mercy of God that those who hear believe and those who believe are saved; but that dullness or hardening comes from sin to those who do not believe; and that the Gentiles were grafted into the grace of God contrary to nature, since from him and through him and in him are all things.
Canon XXVI. That sin and death came upon all people through Adam, and that death reigned from Adam until Moses.
That evil conversations corrupt good morals, and that disputes and quarrels ruin those who hear them rather than build them up.
That the desire to sin, that is, the will of the flesh, which through long habit is now called a law and a nature, is always opposed to the holy will.
That the flesh and its prudence are hostile to God and always keep away from God and from every good.
That our mortal bodies are given life through the Spirit of God dwelling in us.

That the new man is the inner man, whose image is heavenly. He was formed in the image of God and is re-formed by the grace of God and the light of knowledge; like a treasure in an earthen vessel, he is clothed with heartfelt mercy, with faith and with love.
That the old man is the outer man, who is being corrupted, and in whom the body of sin is destroyed; the apostle calls him an earthly house and an earthen vessel.

That the bodies of the saints are temples of God, or of the Holy Spirit, and members of Christ. Therefore they ought always to be a living and pleasing sacrifice, and to keep themselves from every work of the flesh, from whispering, from idle talk and from all other sins; and virgins, following the apostle's counsel, should remain as they are.
That the saints crucify their flesh with its vices and desires, glorying in the cross of Christ, through whom they have died to the world and its works.

That when some abstain from meat and wine, they ought neither to be judged by others nor to judge others themselves, because to the pure all things are pure, and because food and drink commend no one to God. For God, he says, will destroy both the one and the other.
That wine is the whole cause of debauchery, and that one must therefore abstain from it, since he permits its use only for illness, and even then in moderation.
That through blessed voluntary poverty the righteous reject avarice, the root of all evils, content with their daily provision and with enough to cover them, supplied to them through godliness.
That the warfare of the righteous, their weapons, their enemies, and their wrestling or fighting, are spiritual. Their citizenship is in heaven, and from there they await Christ the Lord.
That the work of a teacher is reading and the preaching of the gospel, in which the apostle laboured night and day.
That one ought to persevere in psalms, hymns and spiritual songs and in prayers, both for one another and for kings and for all people.

That the apostle became all things to all people in order to win all, and in this way he pleased everyone. He ought to be imitated, so that Christians may shine like lights among others by their way of life; and their deeds should match their words.
That if anyone receives unworthily the body and blood of Christ, which is the great mystery of godliness, manifested in the flesh and justified in the spirit, he is guilty of that body and blood.
That both the apostle and those to whom he gave thanks were full of knowledge, of faith and of the fragrance of holiness.

That through the manifold grace of the Holy Spirit spiritual gifts have been distributed to the saints as was fitting; that therefore each person ought to remain in the calling in which he was called; and that those of lower rank ought to give honour to those who work together for the gospel.

That a bishop ought to be blameless, and all the clergy peaceable, fleeing youthful desires, keeping the commandment, approving what is better, rebuking the one who goes astray, teaching what is useful; and that old men and widows ought to be likewise.

That churchmen ought not to go to the public courts to defend themselves, but only to the church's courts; that they ought to judge nothing unjustly and to establish a matter by the testimony of two or three witnesses; for the saints will judge the world and the angels.
Canon XLVII. That those who are stronger in faith ought to bear with the weaker, looking to themselves, lest they too be tempted.
That in the orders of the church God chose first apostles, second prophets, third teachers.
That every good thing is to be chosen, and brotherly love is to be preferred to all the virtues; that the time is to be redeemed; and that Christians are to pursue peace and humility.
That those are to be avoided who do not live according to the apostle's tradition but rather serve their own belly; such people will be at their very worst in the last times.
That those who judge others while doing worse things themselves sin more gravely; and that those who consent in any way to sinners are surely partners of those who sin.
That there have been, or will be, false apostles and false prophets, through whom sects arise; and that Satan disguises himself as an angel of light. [?]
That many idle talkers have departed from the apostles, and through them heresies have arisen, leading to error.
That he commends those who labour with him in the gospel and all who preside; their names, as he says, are written in the book of life.
That believers are saved and justified not through the law but through faith in Christ and confession of him, free from the yoke of slavery and from the distinction of the sexes.

Canon LVI. That he commands the people to be subject to the authorities and to work with their own hands; that they should love their wives, children and slaves, and that slaves should love their masters; and that women should be silent in church and not presume to teach.
That he bids those who lack self-control to marry, and that a woman will be saved through bearing children.
That believers are justified by deeds, not by words alone; for the kingdom of God, he says, is not in word but in power.

That the head of a man is Christ, and the head of a woman is the man; that one ought always to pray without anger or quarrelling; and that women ought to be adorned not with necklaces but with their way of life.
That the apostle gives thanks to those who are ready to give alms, and urges others to this work.
That the apostle bears witness to the good life of certain lay people, and to their faith and kindness, because they refreshed either him or the poor among the saints.

That Paul reproaches the avarice of certain people, saying that he preached the gospel to them in such a way as not to burden them; and yet that those who serve the altar ought to live from it, as a soldier lives on his pay.
That certain people risked their necks for the apostle, and that not only he but all the churches give thanks to them; and they also received churches in their own homes.

Canon LXIV. That those who pursue the righteousness of the law are ignorant of the righteousness of God, which was given through Christ; for it was impossible for those who served the law to take away their sins.

That the apostle says there are two laws: one through Moses, which is carnal, and the other through faith and the grace of Christ, which is spiritual. He abolishes the first because it does not justify, but establishes the second because it saves and sanctifies.
That in the Jewish law there is a curse, from which Christ frees us by becoming a curse himself.
That through the spiritual circumcision of the heart in Christ the apostle abolishes that shameful circumcision of the law.
That the things done or written in the Old Testament happened as figures of us.

That the apostle sets before the Jews the faith of Abraham to be imitated, showing that believers are justified not by the works of the law but by the works of faith; and he calls them the Israel of God.

That the Gentiles ought not to boast over the fall of the Jews. For God wills all people to be saved; he has shut up all things under sin so that he may have mercy on all; and through Christ he has reconciled us to himself. For God, he says, was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself.

That although he accuses himself of having been a persecutor of the churches and calls himself the least of the apostles, he nevertheless declares that he was caught up to the third heaven. There, without doubt, he was instructed in the gospel, which he says he was taught not by any human being but by Christ, through the revelation of the Spirit.

That the same apostle says he received the grace of apostleship from God, and that Christ speaks and works in him; and that those who are led by the Spirit of God are the children of God, heirs of God and fellow heirs with Christ.
That he preached the gospel where none of the apostles had been, and that he was sent by Christ to preach the gospel.
That he did no less than the other apostles, both in preaching and in signs; for, he says, even if I am unskilled in speech, I am not so in knowledge.
That he is the apostle of the Gentiles, to whom he also preaches the gospel; that when he came to Antioch he rebuked Peter; and that James and John gave him and Barnabas the right hand of fellowship.
That he had Timothy as a colleague, Epaphroditus as a fellow apostle and fellow soldier, and other helpers or ministers.

That he calls "sons" those whom he was instructing in the knowledge of the truth. Among them he used the power of his apostolic authority, and he rejoices over those whom he had grieved into repentance.

That he was sent by Christ to preach rather than to baptize; and that in baptism we have been buried with Christ, so that, having been made sons of God, we may walk in newness of life, heirs of God and joint heirs with Christ.

That because of the enormity of their sins wicked people are handed over to worse passions; that the creation was not subjected willingly; that no other creature separates us from the love of Christ; and that the gospel has been preached to the creation.
That he said that he knows in part and prophesies in part, and sees through a mirror the things that are to come, as he runs toward the prize of God's heavenly calling.
That Christians ought to rejoice in their sufferings, knowing that their faith is a gift of God; for suffering for Christ will bring an eternal reward.

That in the general resurrection the bodies of the saints will be clothed in different degrees of glory, according to their merits. There flesh and blood, that is, the works of the belly and of lust, will no longer reign.
That Christ is the firstfruits of the resurrection, and after him come those who belong to him; and that he now sits above every principality and power, placed at the Father's right hand.

That he says that people still living in the body have risen in baptism: those who are dead to sin have been made alive together with Christ and seek the things that are above, not the things on earth.

That there will be a judgment of God with Christ as the just judge. There each person will receive according to his works, and conscience will give an account even of his thoughts. All who are guilty of crimes will undergo the scrutiny of God as judge.
That those who do not honor God are dishonored by God and abandoned to their own desires, to be judged all the more severely.
That before the day of judgment the son of sin will come, who is understood to be the Antichrist.

That the judgment at the end of the world will be by fire, which he also calls wrath. That day will come like a thief at the coming of Jesus from heaven, upon the sons of disobedience and upon all ungodliness.

That the present happiness of this world is to be spurned, not only because it is brief but because it is harmful and wicked; and that its wisdom is foolishness. "Among these things," he says, "we too once lived." And that death is to be destroyed last, when the righteous have received from the Lord vengeance on those who now afflict them.
That the righteous will reign forever with God the Father and with Christ, where the body will no longer be subject to corruption.
